story.title: The Air the Second-Born Held
story.deck: On the refinery moon Calder, eight hundred engineered workers with no standing have set the air plants to a slow decline, and Illuminara must find a guarantee strong enough that nobody has to hold a breath hostage again.
story.shape: Five days of a countdown; each scene moves one party's line of dependence into the open until the air itself becomes the guarantee.

scenes.title: The Gate Below Nine
paragraphs: *Lower Level Nine, Ring Gate · Day one, 06:10*
Wren Odira read the numbers off the slate before the lift had finished opening.

**Wren Odira**  
Plant Two is at eighty-two percent of demand and losing two points a day. The tanks cover the gap, but only down to seventy-four. Under that, if any deck on Calder takes a hull breach, there is not enough reserve to repressurize it.

**Illuminara**  
And Plant One?

**Wren Odira**  
Forty-one percent of the colony's air, and the engineers say it cannot be pushed past forty-nine. Plant Two is the rest. Kesh Aurelian sequences Plant Two. He said five days, and at two points a day, five days is the line.

The corridor beyond the gate was low and warm and smelled of hot metal and boiled grain. Illuminara stood in it and let AC do what it did. It did not read minds. It made the lines of force in a place visible to her, the way a map makes slope visible, and she saw how the people in the corridor leaned. Every body leaned toward the gate. It was not the lean of hostility. It was the posture of people who had been told, all their lives, to wait.

*That is a reading, and a reading is a guess about someone else's mouth. Test it before you rest on it.* She had been a court interpreter at twenty-four. She had learned that the first meaning always arrives sounding like certainty.
A woman in a grey scrubber-hall coat came out of the crowd and did not offer her hand.

**Marit Voss**  
Marit Voss. I run the day shift on Two. Kesh said you would ask to see him first.

**Illuminara**  
I would like to start with whoever has to breathe the answer.

**Marit Voss**  
That is the wrong answer for a diplomat and I may keep you for it. There are eight hundred of us on this plant. We have run it since before the first of us was born, legally speaking. Come to the hall tonight. They will ask you things. If you answer like a politician nobody opens that door twice.

scenes.title: What the Hall Asked
paragraphs: *Scrubber Hall, Plant Two · Day one, 20:00*

They sat on the maintenance benches among the great grey cylinders, three hundred of them, the rest listening on the relay. The elder, Osei Tamm, had a voice like a worn gasket and did not stand to speak.

**Osei Tamm**  
Ninth Year, the council gave us a charter. Recognition, they called it. We were counted. We were given ration cards with our own names on them. In nineteen months they repealed it, and the census reclassified us as contract stock, and the cards stopped working at the canteen. I was forty. I remember the canteen.

**Illuminara**  
And since then, every recognition has been used and then taken back.

**Osei Tamm**  
Every one. Do not say it as if you have learned it from a file. The one thing on this moon they cannot repeal is the air, because it passes through our hands. That is not politics. It is the only fact we have.

**Marit Voss**  
Ask her what you want to ask her, Teodor. You have been holding it all day.
A young man near the back stood up. His hands were scarred across the knuckles from valve work.

**Teodor Rask**  
My sister is on Level Four. First-born husband, a baby. I turn the dials that are going down. I am not going to tell you I am proud of it. If this ends with a child on Four in a tent, I did that, and Kesh did that, and I do not know what I am if the price of being a person is that.
Nobody spoke. Marit turned toward the room.

**Marit Voss**  
I am not a lever. I want that said in front of her. I want my standing. I do not want it bought with somebody's lungs. If the only way we get it is by being the hand on the throat, then they were right about us and I would rather lose.

**Osei Tamm**  
Then you will lose, Marit. Sit down. Both things are true.
Illuminara waited until the room had finished being angry. Then she said what she had, which was less than they wanted.

**Illuminara**  
I do not know yet how to give you a guarantee that cannot be taken back. I know three things. I know I cannot ask you to trust me. I know the air has been your only leverage and your worst burden. And I know that if I find nothing, I will say so plainly, and you will have lost nothing but two days.

**Osei Tamm**  
Two days. That is an honest sum. Come back when you have something that does not need us to like you.

scenes.title: The Number Behind the Council
paragraphs: *Council Chamber, Upper Ring · Day two, 09:15*
Speaker Ines Torvald had a clipped, tired manner and did not rise either.

**Ines Torvald**  
We do not bargain with hostage-takers. If we do, the next group learns the shape of the key. I will hear you out. I will not promise you a concession.

**Illuminara**  
I am not asking you to bargain. I am asking what happens on day five.
Chief Engineer Dov Hallam unrolled a section of the plant schematic across the table. He spoke like a man reading a charge sheet against his own drawings.

**Dov Hallam**  
Day five is seventy-four percent. Below that there is no breach margin. I have a cross-feed from the upper tank farm that would let us seal the upper decks' reserve and let the lower ones go short. It holds sixty thousand minus the lower levels. I drew it at six this morning because it was the thing I could draw.

**Illuminara**  
Then it is a verdict, not a reserve. Fourteen thousand people live below Nine. They did not set the plants. Seal everyone or seal no one.

**Pell Arkwright**  
The owners will lose four days of throughput if you ration the ore plant to hold the margin for all decks. I am obliged to say so.

**Illuminara**  
Say it and then do it. The cost is real. It is also smaller than a deck that cannot be repressurized.
Dov looked at the cross-feed line, then at her, and rolled it differently, so that the reserve fed all decks to the same floor.

**Dov Hallam**  
Rationing the ore plant by half gives me margin to hold seventy-four for all of them to about day seven. It buys two days. It does not solve anything.

**Illuminara**  
It means no child on Four has to depend on what Kesh decides on day five. That matters even if he decides well.

While they argued the rationing, AC showed her something else. Three lines of dependence ran across the room, from the council, from the owners, from the engineer, and all three ran toward the same place and none of the three looked at it. It was the Registry certificate on the wall behind Dov, off-moon authority, the plant's operating license.
*A hypothesis. Do not say it as a fact.*

**Illuminara**  
Dov. What does the certificate say about who may run the plant?

**Dov Hallam**  
Registry-certified operators. It says nothing about class. The second-born are certified under contract-labor codes because nobody here ever put the question to the Registry. If the council repealed everything tomorrow, the Registry would still hold eight hundred certified operators on its books.

**Illuminara**  
And if the council declared them uncertified?

**Dov Hallam**  
The plant loses its certificate. The insurance lapses with it. Then Pell cannot sell a barrel.
Pell Arkwright said nothing, which was an answer.

**Illuminara**  
Then there is a cost to repeal that does not depend on anyone on Calder being kind. I will test whether it is as strong as it sounds. I will test it with the man who has the most reason to doubt it.

scenes.title: The Key and the Throat
paragraphs: *Plant Two Control Room · Day three, 14:00*

Kesh Aurelian was tall in the way that engineered people sometimes were, designed for a height nobody had asked for, and he stood with his back to the sequencing console as if guarding it from her. Hana Duvall, a nurse from the Level Four clinic, had come up with Illuminara. Illuminara had asked for a first-born resident. Hana had asked for the room.

**Kesh Aurelian**  
You have been on my moon for three days and the first thing you do is give the council a way to ration around me.

**Illuminara**  
Yes. And I told you within the hour, because if you had found it yourself on day four, you would never have believed anything I said after.

**Kesh Aurelian**  
You hedged my five days.

**Illuminara**  
I protected the people who were not part of the argument. That is not the same as protecting them from you. It protects them from the arithmetic.
Kesh took that. His hands, at his sides, did not move.

**Kesh Aurelian**  
Say what you came to say.

**Illuminara**  
The council will pay, but they can pay in a currency that does not need goodwill. The plant's operating certificate comes from the Registry, off-moon, and it names qualified operators, not citizens. Eight hundred of them are yours. Repeal their standing and the plant loses its certificate, the insurance lapses, and the owners cannot sell. That is a cost the council cannot waive and the owners cannot absorb.

**Kesh Aurelian**  
And if the Registry changes its mind?

**Illuminara**  
Then the guarantee depends on the Registry. It is the one body here that is neither the council, nor the owners, nor you, nor me.

**Kesh Aurelian**  
That is still goodwill. Different address. Show me a guarantee that does not depend on anyone's goodwill, including yours. If I hand back the air for a promise, my people are one election from the mines again.
Illuminara said nothing for a moment. The room hummed. *He is not asking to rule. Watch what he is asking for.* He did not want the chair. He wanted the thing nobody could take back.

**Illuminara**  
You are right. A charter is only as strong as the cost of breaking it. So I do not ask you to hand back the key. I ask you to share it. Every shift on Plant Two is run by two people, one second-born and one other, and any shutdown or sequence change needs both. The air stops being your leverage. It becomes everyone's duty, and a repeal would have to take that duty apart in front of the Registry.

**Kesh Aurelian**  
You are asking me to give up the only key I have and calling it a gift.

**Illuminara**  
I am asking you to give up the only key you have. I am not calling it a gift. It costs you your hand on the throat. It costs the council sole control. It costs the owners a cheap labour class. It costs you in front of your own people.
Hana had been standing against the wall. She spoke without moving off it.

**Hana Duvall**  
I am not here to be your lever either. I walked up here to tell you that. My clinic put the neonatal ward in oxygen tents last night. Anselm Pruitt died at four this morning. He was seventy-one. His lungs had two years left and now they have none.

**Kesh Aurelian**  
I read the list.

**Hana Duvall**  
Then you know the name.

**Kesh Aurelian**  
Anselm Pruitt. Yes.

He did not defend it. Illuminara watched him not defend it, and watched the old reflex that said every harm was the fault of those who had made harm necessary rise and die in his throat. He said, quietly, to the room:

**Kesh Aurelian**  
I would hold the plants at seventy-four and not a point lower. I set the line myself. I did not set it to kill a man. A man is dead anyway.

**Hana Duvall**  
Yes. Now you decide what that means.

scenes.title: The Count
paragraphs: *Ballot Hall, Lower Level Seven · Day four, 19:30*

The second-born voted without Kesh in the room. Marit had insisted, and Osei Tamm had agreed, and Kesh had gone and sat in the plant corridor with his arms folded and looked at nothing. Illuminara stood at the back with Wren and held her tongue while eight hundred people raised their hands under the grey lights.
The elders counted. Marit counted twice.

**Osei Tamm**  
Six hundred and twelve for. A hundred and forty-eight against. Forty abstain.

**Teodor Rask**  
I voted against. A certificate is not a citizenship. It is a floor under the work, not a door into the house.

**Illuminara**  
You are right. It is a floor. It is not a door. I would rather say that now than have you find it in a year.

**Teodor Rask**  
Then why did you ask us to vote?

**Illuminara**  
Because I do not get to decide for you what is enough. I get to put an honest thing in front of you, and you get to hold it up and see how it looks.

The Registry duty officer, Sabine Okafor-Reyes, appeared on the relay at 20:10 with the signed amendment: Plant Two's certificate would carry the joint-shift requirement as a condition of operation, effective on restoration. Teodor, who read cryptographic signatures for fun, checked the Registry's key against the amendment on his own console. Kesh called the duty officer on a line the council did not control and listened to her say the same words twice.

**Kesh Aurelian**  
She says the amendment stands whether the council signs the charter or not.

**Illuminara**  
It does. I would not give you anything that needed the council's signature to exist.

**Kesh Aurelian**  
Then I stand down first. Before the charter. Before any reward.

**Illuminara**  
That is the order I wanted.

The council did not sign that night. Ines Torvald sent word that she would sign at dawn and not before, as if the hour were hers. Illuminara decided that did not matter. The stand-down was Kesh's to make. The signing was the council's to be seen making. Different currencies.

scenes.title: Seventy-Four
paragraphs: *Scrubber Hall, Plant Two · Day five, 02:40*

Marit and a council engineer named Jun Calloway sat shoulder to shoulder at the sequencing console, each with a key on a chain round the neck, and neither would look at the other. Jun's hands shook. Marit's did not.
Kesh took the open channel and spoke into it the way a man pulls a splinter.

**Kesh Aurelian**  
This is Kesh Aurelian. At 02:41 I release the sequencing on Plant Two. I set the plants to decline. A man named Anselm Pruitt is dead of it. I will answer to the Registry's inquiry and to the people of Level Four. The air belongs to all of you now. It always did.
He turned the key in his own lock and set it in Marit's palm. Jun turned his. The console accepted the pair.
The numbers began to climb. Wren read them out softly, as if loud voices might stall them.

**Wren Odira**  
Seventy-six. Seventy-nine. Eighty-two. The tanks are drawing down.

**Marit Voss**  
Hold it there. Let it rise on its own, not on mine or his.
Osei Tamm stood at the back of the hall with his arms crossed. He did not look pleased, and Illuminara had not expected him to.

**Osei Tamm**  
A certificate is not a home. A floor is not a house.

**Illuminara**  
No. It is where you start from, and nobody can pull it out from under you without paying for it in front of strangers. That is less than you deserve. It is more than you had on Monday.

**Osei Tamm**  
Hmph. It is a start. I will eat my cap if they keep the second key when the owners change.

**Illuminara**  
Then the Registry will have the owners to deal with, and you will have Marit to ask.
Hana Duvall came down at 03:30 with a thermos and set it on the console without a word, between two keys. Marit looked at it, and at her, and nodded once. Nothing was forgiven. It was only shared.

By 04:10 Plant Two was at ninety-six percent of demand, the seventy-four line a long way below them, the tanks refilling, and the reserve for every deck on Calder, upper and lower, held to the same floor. The council would sign at dawn. The resentment in the hall would last longer than the signing, and Illuminara did not mind that, because resentment was an honest instrument and it was pointed at something real.
Marit leaned back from the console and breathed in, long, as if testing that it was hers.

**Marit Voss**  
Two keys.

**Illuminara**  
Two keys.

Kesh took that. His hands, at his sides, did not move.

**Kesh Aurelian**  
Say what you came to say.

**Illuminara**  
The eight hundred have never been filed as operators of record. The owners put them on the contract-labour schedule, and the council has been able to do to them what a clerk did in the Ninth Year. Refile them under Article Six. Each of you gets a record the Registry keeps off-moon: your name, not a stock number, your post, your contract in your own hand. You can be moved only by a finding of cause after a hearing. And on the console itself, every shift run by two operators, one second-born and one other, and any sequence change needs both keys.

**Kesh Aurelian**  
Then I will tell you how they beat it. Tell me where I am wrong. They bring in first-born operators and let ours lapse unused.

**Illuminara**  
A post of record cannot be vacated except by the panel. A cut of more than a tenth of a crew opens a public hearing, a hundred and eighty days.

**Kesh Aurelian**  
The census puts us back to contract stock.

**Illuminara**  
The census is the council's. The record is the Registry's.

**Kesh Aurelian**  
Pell sells the plant to someone who does not care.

**Illuminara**  
The licence cannot pass without the operators of record. The buyer takes the eight hundred with the plant, or buys nothing.

**Kesh Aurelian**  
They change the article.

**Illuminara**  
Two-thirds of forty settlements, in open session, after a hundred and eighty days. It can be done. It cannot be done quietly. The Ninth Year took nineteen months of quiet. This would take a year of daylight.

**Kesh Aurelian**  
A year of daylight is still a year. And it is still other people's goodwill.

**Illuminara**  
It is other people's interest. Six settlements stand on the same article. Goodwill has to be asked for. Interest only has to be noticed.
Kesh looked at the console, not at her. It was the first time he had looked away from her since she came in.

**Kesh Aurelian**  
Say all of that holds. You still hand me a console with two keys on it. What stops the next Kesh? What stops Jun, or Pell's man, who sits on his key until a bearing fails and says the second-born made him do it? Joint control is a veto in two hands. A hostage needs a hand and a throat. You have given the hands a new throat.

Illuminara did not answer at once. *He is not asking to rule. Watch what he is asking for.* He did not want the chair. He wanted the thing nobody could take back, and he had just found the flaw in her own design faster than she had.

**Illuminara**  
You are right. I built that wrong. A veto over the air is still a lever. So take the lever out of the keys. Dov's old trip, the one that forbids sequencing below ninety percent of rating. We put it back, and the Registry seals it, not the council and not you. The keys never decide whether air flows. They decide only when a maintenance window may open, above the floor, with seventy-two hours' notice posted to every deck.

**Kesh Aurelian**  
And below the floor?

**Illuminara**  
Nothing lowers it. Break the seal and every deck's alarm sounds and the Registry duty office is paged. The seal holds six hours and then the plant reverts on its own. **Kesh Aurelian**  
Jun withholds his key to stop a repair. The bearing fails.

**Illuminara**

**Kesh Aurelian**  
So the key can only keep the air on.

scenes.title: The Count
paragraphs: *Ballot Hall, Lower Level Seven · Day four, 19:30*

The second-born voted without Kesh in the room. Marit had insisted, and Osei Tamm had agreed, and Kesh had gone and sat in the plant corridor with his arms folded and looked at nothing. Illuminara stood at the back with Wren and held her tongue while eight hundred people raised their hands under the grey lights.
The elders counted. Marit counted twice.

**Osei Tamm**  
Six hundred and twelve for. A hundred and forty-eight against. Forty abstain.

**Teodor Rask**  
I voted against. A record is not a vote. It is a floor under the work, and a name on a shelf off-moon. It is not a door into the house.

**Illuminara**  
You are right. It is standing of record: your name, your post, a hearing before anyone can move you. It is not a seat on the council and I will not call it one. I would rather say that now than have you find it in a year.

**Teodor Rask**  
Then why did you ask us to vote?

**Illuminara**  
Because I do not get to decide for you what is enough. I get to put an honest thing in front of you, and you get to hold it up and see how it looks.

**Marit Voss**

Beside her signature stood another.

**Pell Arkwright**  
I am obliged to countersign as licence-holder. I find I am relieved to.

Teodor, who read cryptographic signatures for fun, checked the Registry's key against the refiling on his own console. Kesh called the duty officer on a line the council did not control and listened to her say the same words twice.

**Kesh Aurelian**  
She says the refiling stands whether the council signs the charter or not.

**Illuminara**

**Kesh Aurelian**

**Illuminara**

scenes.title: Seventy-Four
paragraphs: *Scrubber Hall, Plant Two · Day five, 02:40*

Marit and a council engineer named Jun Calloway sat shoulder to shoulder at the sequencing console, each with a key on a chain round the neck, and neither would look at the other. Jun's hands shook. Marit's did not.
Kesh took the open channel and spoke into it the way a man pulls a splinter.

**Kesh Aurelian**

He turned the key in his own lock and set it in Marit's palm. Jun turned his. The console accepted the pair, and the Registry's seal came up green on the bus.
The numbers began to climb. Nobody had to turn a key to raise them. Wren read them out softly, as if loud voices might stall them.

**Wren Odira**  
Seventy-six. Seventy-nine. Eighty-two. The tanks are drawing down.

**Marit Voss**  
Hold it there. Let it rise on its own, not on mine or his.

**Jun Calloway**  
I came up here afraid of what you would do with that key.

**Marit Voss**  
I was afraid of the same about yours.

**Jun Calloway**  
I could not lower it now if I tried. Could I?

**Dov Hallam**

**Osei Tamm**

**Osei Tamm**

**Illuminara**

**Hana Duvall**

Marit looked at the thermos, and at her, and nodded once. Nothing was forgiven. It was only shared.

She leaned back from the console and breathed in, long, as if testing that it was hers.

**Marit Voss**  
Two keys.

**Illuminara**  
Two keys.

story.title: The Air the Second-Born Held
story.deck: On the refinery moon Calder, eight hundred engineered workers with no standing have set the air plants to a slow decline, and Illuminara must find a guarantee strong enough that nobody has to hold a breath hostage again, and a standing no council can vote away.
story.shape: Five days of a countdown; each scene moves one party's line of dependence into the open until the air rests on a lever nobody can pull, and the second-born's standing rests on a record no one on Calder keeps.

scenes.title: The Gate Below Nine
paragraphs: *Lower Level Nine, Ring Gate · Day one, 06:10*
Wren Odira read the numbers off the slate before the lift had finished opening.

**Wren Odira**  
Plant Two is at eighty-two percent of rating and losing two points a day. Oxygen from the tanks covers the gap, but only down to seventy-four. Under that there is not enough reserve to repressurize a deck that takes a breach.

**Illuminara**  
And what the tanks cannot cover?

**Wren Odira**  
The tanks make oxygen. They do not scrub. Level Four read four thousand parts per million of carbon dioxide at midnight. The norm is fifteen hundred.

**Illuminara**  
Who lives on Four?

**Wren Odira**  
The clinic. The nursery. The old. It is the dead end of the ring, so it fills first, and the clinic's last ward sits past the final vent where the air barely moves.

**Illuminara**  
And Plant One?

**Wren Odira**  
Forty-one percent of the colony's air, and the engineers say it cannot be pushed past forty-nine. Plant Two is the rest, and it feeds the lower ring. Kesh Aurelian sequences Plant Two. He said day five, and at two points a day, day five is the line.

The corridor beyond the gate was low and warm and smelled of hot metal and boiled grain. Illuminara stood in it and let AC do what it did. It did not read minds. It made the lines of force in a place visible to her, the way a map makes slope visible, and she saw how the people in the corridor leaned. Every body leaned toward the gate. It was not the lean of hostility. It was the posture of people who had been told, all their lives, to wait.

*That is a reading, and a reading is a guess about someone else's mouth. Test it before you rest on it.* She had been a court interpreter at twenty-four. She had learned that the first meaning always arrives sounding like certainty.
A woman in a grey scrubber-hall coat came out of the crowd and did not offer her hand.

**Marit Voss**  
Marit Voss. I run the day shift on Two. Kesh said you would ask to see him first.

**Illuminara**  
I would like to start with whoever has to breathe the answer.

**Marit Voss**  
That is the wrong answer for a diplomat and I may keep you for it. There are eight hundred of us on this plant. We have run it since before the first of us was born, legally speaking. Come to the hall tonight. They will ask you things. If you answer like a politician nobody opens that door twice.

scenes.title: What the Hall Asked
paragraphs: *Scrubber Hall, Plant Two · Day one, 20:00*

They sat on the maintenance benches among the great grey cylinders, three hundred of them, the rest listening on the relay. The elder, Osei Tamm, had a voice like a worn gasket and did not stand to speak.

**Osei Tamm**  
Ninth Year, the council gave us a charter. Recognition, they called it. We were counted. We were given ration cards with our own names on them. In nineteen months they repealed it. They did not even need a vote against us. A clerk added a column to the census, and we were contract stock again, and the cards stopped working at the canteen. I was forty. I remember the canteen.

**Illuminara**  
And since then, every recognition has been used and then taken back.

**Osei Tamm**  
Every one. Do not say it as if you have learned it from a file. The one thing on this moon they cannot repeal is the air, because it passes through our hands. That is not politics. It is the only fact we have.

**Marit Voss**  
Ask her what you want to ask her, Teodor. You have been holding it all day.
A young man near the back stood up. His hands were scarred across the knuckles from valve work.

**Teodor Rask**

Nobody spoke. Marit turned toward the room.

I am not a lever. I want that said in front of her. I want my standing. I do not want it bought with somebody's lungs. If the only way we get it is by being the hand on the throat, then they were right about us and I would rather lose.

**Osei Tamm**  
Then you will lose, Marit. Sit down. Both things are true.
Illuminara waited until the room had finished being angry. Then she said what she had, which was less than they wanted.

**Illuminara**  
I do not know yet how to give you a guarantee that cannot be taken back. I know three things. I know I cannot ask you to trust me. I know the air has been your only leverage and your worst burden. And I know that if I find nothing, I will say so plainly, and you will have lost nothing but two days.

**Osei Tamm**  
Two days. That is an honest sum. Come back when you have something that does not need us to like you.

scenes.title: The Number Behind the Council
paragraphs: *Council Chamber, Upper Ring · Day two, 09:15*
Speaker Ines Torvald had a clipped, tired manner and did not rise either.

**Illuminara**  
Then it is a verdict, not a reserve. Fourteen thousand people live below Nine. They did not set the plants. Seal everyone or seal no one.

**Pell Arkwright**

**Illuminara**  
Say it and then do it. The cost is real. It is also smaller than a deck that cannot be repressurized.
Dov looked at the cross-feed line, then at her, and rolled it differently, so that the reserve fed all decks to the same floor.

**Dov Hallam**

**Illuminara**  
Then someone on Four has a bad night first.

**Dov Hallam**  
Yes. I would rather say it than have you find it.

It was the Registry certificate on the wall behind Dov, off-moon authority, the plant's operating licence.
*A hypothesis. Do not say it as a fact.*

**Illuminara**  
Dov. What does the certificate say about who may run the plant?

**Dov Hallam**

**Illuminara**  
What does the Registry do with an operator it has certified?

**Dov Hallam**

**Illuminara**  
And the article itself? Who can change that?

**Dov Hallam**

**Dov Hallam**

**Dov Hallam**

**Illuminara**  
Keep it. I may want it back.
She turned back to the table, and to the room that had begun, a little, to lean toward the same place.

**Illuminara**

**Illuminara**

**Kesh Aurelian**

**Illuminara**  
The census is the council's. The record is the Registry's.

**Kesh Aurelian**  
Pell sells the plant to someone who does not care.

**Illuminara**  
The licence cannot pass without the operators of record. The buyer takes the eight hundred with the plant, or buys nothing.

**Kesh Aurelian**  
They change the article.

**Illuminara**

**Kesh Aurelian**

**Illuminara**

**Kesh Aurelian**  
Six hours is still six hours.

**Illuminara**

**Kesh Aurelian**  
Jun withholds his key to stop a repair. The bearing fails.

**Illuminara**

**Kesh Aurelian**

**Hana Duvall**

**Kesh Aurelian**

He did not defend it. Illuminara watched him not defend it, and watched the old reflex that said every harm was the fault of those who had made harm necessary rise and die in his throat. He said, quietly, to the room:

I wrote the word acceptable in my notes. A man's name sits under that word now, beside whatever else was wrong with him.

Two keys.

story.title: The Air the Second-Born Held
story.deck: On the refinery moon Calder, eight hundred engineered workers with no standing have set the air plants to a slow decline, and Illuminara must find a guarantee strong enough that nobody has to hold a breath hostage again, and a standing no council can vote away.
story.shape: Five days of a countdown; each scene moves one party's line of dependence into the open until the air rests on a lever nobody can pull, and the second-born's standing rests on a record no one on Calder keeps.

scenes.title: The Gate Below Nine
paragraphs: *Lower Level Nine, Ring Gate · Day one, 06:10*
Wren Odira read the numbers off the slate before the lift had finished opening.

**Wren Odira**  
Plant Two is at eighty-two percent of rating and losing two points a day. Oxygen from the tanks covers the gap, but only down to seventy-four. Under that there is not enough reserve to repressurize a deck that takes a breach.

**Illuminara**  
And what the tanks cannot cover?

**Wren Odira**  
The tanks make oxygen. They do not scrub. Level Four read four thousand parts per million of carbon dioxide at midnight. The norm is fifteen hundred.

**Illuminara**  
Who lives on Four?

**Wren Odira**  
The clinic. The nursery. The old. It is the dead end of the ring, so it fills first, and the clinic's last ward sits past the final vent where the air barely moves.

**Illuminara**  
And Plant One?

**Wren Odira**  
Forty-one percent of the colony's air, and the engineers say it cannot be pushed past forty-nine. Plant Two is the rest, and it feeds the lower ring. Kesh Aurelian sequences Plant Two. He said day five, and at two points a day, day five is the line.

The corridor beyond the gate was low and warm and smelled of hot metal and boiled grain. Illuminara stood in it and let AC do what it did. It did not read minds. It made the lines of force in a place visible to her, the way a map makes slope visible, and she saw how the people in the corridor leaned. Every body leaned toward the gate. It was not the lean of hostility. It was the posture of people who had been told, all their lives, to wait.

*That is a reading, and a reading is a guess about someone else's mouth. Test it before you rest on it.* She had been a court interpreter at twenty-four. She had learned that the first meaning always arrives sounding like certainty.
A woman in a grey scrubber-hall coat came out of the crowd and did not offer her hand.

**Marit Voss**  
Marit Voss. I run the day shift on Two. Kesh said you would ask to see him first.

**Illuminara**  
I would like to start with whoever has to breathe the answer.

**Marit Voss**  
That is the wrong answer for a diplomat and I may keep you for it. There are eight hundred of us on this plant. We have run it since before the first of us was born, legally speaking. Come to the hall tonight. They will ask you things. If you answer like a politician nobody opens that door twice.

scenes.title: What the Hall Asked
paragraphs: *Scrubber Hall, Plant Two · Day one, 20:00*

They sat on the maintenance benches among the great grey cylinders, three hundred of them, the rest listening on the relay. The elder, Osei Tamm, had a voice like a worn gasket and did not stand to speak.

**Osei Tamm**  
Ninth Year, the council gave us a charter. Recognition, they called it. We were counted. We were given ration cards with our own names on them. In nineteen months they repealed it. They did not even need a vote against us. A clerk added a column to the census, and we were contract stock again, and the cards stopped working at the canteen. I was forty. I remember the canteen.

**Illuminara**  
And since then, every recognition has been used and then taken back.

**Osei Tamm**  
Every one. Do not say it as if you have learned it from a file. The one thing on this moon they cannot repeal is the air, because it passes through our hands. That is not politics. It is the only fact we have.

**Marit Voss**  
Ask her what you want to ask her, Teodor. You have been holding it all day.
A young man near the back stood up. His hands were scarred across the knuckles from valve work.

**Teodor Rask**  
My sister is on Level Four. First-born husband, a baby. The ring read forty-one hundred when I came off shift, and I turn the dials that are going down. I am not going to tell you I am proud of it. If this ends with a child on Four in a tent, I did that, and Kesh did that, and I do not know what I am if the price of being a person is that.
Nobody spoke. Marit turned toward the room.

**Marit Voss**  
I am not a lever. I want that said in front of her. I want my standing. I do not want it bought with somebody's lungs. If the only way we get it is by being the hand on the throat, then they were right about us and I would rather lose.

**Osei Tamm**  
Then you will lose, Marit. Sit down. Both things are true.
Illuminara waited until the room had finished being angry. Then she said what she had, which was less than they wanted.

**Illuminara**  
I do not know yet how to give you a guarantee that cannot be taken back. I know three things. I know I cannot ask you to trust me. I know the air has been your only leverage and your worst burden. And I know that if I find nothing, I will say so plainly, and you will have lost nothing but two days.

**Osei Tamm**  
Two days. That is an honest sum. Come back when you have something that does not need us to like you.

scenes.title: The Number Behind the Council
paragraphs: *Council Chamber, Upper Ring · Day two, 09:15*
Speaker Ines Torvald had a clipped, tired manner and did not rise either.

**Ines Torvald**  
We do not bargain with hostage-takers. If we do, the next group learns the shape of the key. I will hear you out. I will not promise you a concession.

**Illuminara**  
I am not asking you to bargain. I am asking what happens on day five.
Chief Engineer Dov Hallam unrolled a section of the plant schematic across the table. He spoke like a man reading a charge sheet against his own drawings.

**Dov Hallam**  
Day five is seventy-four. Below that there is no breach margin. I have a cross-feed from the upper tank farm that would let me seal the upper decks' reserve and let the lower ones go short. I drew it at six this morning because it was the thing I could draw.

**Illuminara**  
Then it is a verdict, not a reserve. Fourteen thousand people live below Nine. They did not set the plants. Seal everyone or seal no one.

**Pell Arkwright**  
The owners will lose four days of throughput if you ration the ore plant to hold the margin for all decks. I am obliged to say so.

**Illuminara**  
Say it and then do it. The cost is real. It is also smaller than a deck that cannot be repressurized.
Dov looked at the cross-feed line, then at her, and rolled it differently, so that the reserve fed all decks to the same floor.

**Dov Hallam**  
Rationing the ore plant by half holds seventy-four for everyone to about day seven. It also frees the power to wake the old scrubber banks on Four through Seven. They need a day and a quarter. The ring will not have its air back before tomorrow noon.

**Illuminara**  
Then someone on Four has a bad night first.

**Dov Hallam**  
Yes. I would rather say it than have you find it.

While they argued the rationing, AC showed her something else. Three lines of dependence ran across the room, from the council, from the owners, from the engineer, and all three ran toward the same place and none of the three looked at it. It was the Registry certificate on the wall behind Dov, off-moon authority, the plant's operating licence.
*A hypothesis. Do not say it as a fact.*

**Illuminara**  
Dov. What does the certificate say about who may run the plant?

**Dov Hallam**  
Registry-certified operators. It says nothing about class. The second-born run it under the contract-labour schedule because the owners filed them there thirty years ago and nobody since has put the question to the Registry.

**Illuminara**  
What does the Registry do with an operator it has certified?

**Dov Hallam**  
Under Article Six, an operator of record is held by the person, not the employer. Name, number, post. The colony can change a worker's census class. It cannot change a record the Registry keeps. Only a finding of cause from the Registry's Review Panel, after a hearing, can remove one.

**Illuminara**  
And the article itself? Who can change that?

**Dov Hallam**  
Two-thirds of the forty member settlements, in open session, after a hundred and eighty days' notice. Six of them run crews like ours on the same schedule. Nobody here has ever filed a single operator under Six. We have never been in it.
Ines Torvald had stopped looking at her papers.

**Ines Torvald**  
If the Registry recorded them, I could not repeal it by resolution.

**Dov Hallam**  
No. And the insurer would not insure a plant whose operators of record were struck off by a colony vote. Pell could not sell a barrel.
Pell Arkwright said nothing, which was an answer.

**Dov Hallam**  
One more thing, since we are being honest. There is an old safety trip on the sequence bus. It forbids sequencing below ninety percent of rating. We bypassed it years ago because it tripped the plant whenever a bearing ran hot.

**Illuminara**  
Keep it. I may want it back.
She turned back to the table, and to the room that had begun, a little, to lean toward the same place.

**Illuminara**  
Then there is a cost to repeal that does not depend on anyone on Calder being kind. I will test whether it is as strong as it sounds. I will test it with the man who has the most reason to doubt it.

scenes.title: The Key and the Throat
paragraphs: *Plant Two Control Room · Day three, 14:00*

Kesh Aurelian was tall in the way that engineered people sometimes were, designed for a height nobody had asked for, and he stood with his back to the sequencing console as if guarding it from her. Hana Duvall, a nurse from the Level Four clinic, had come up with Illuminara. Illuminara had asked for a first-born resident. Hana had asked for the room.

**Kesh Aurelian**  
You have been on my moon for three days and the first thing you do is give the council a way to ration around me.

**Illuminara**  
Yes. And I told you within the hour, because if you had found it yourself on day four, you would never have believed anything I said after.

**Kesh Aurelian**  
You hedged my five days.

**Illuminara**  
I protected the people who were not part of the argument. That is not the same as protecting them from you. It protects them from the arithmetic.
Kesh took that. His hands, at his sides, did not move.

**Kesh Aurelian**  
Say what you came to say.

**Illuminara**  
The eight hundred have never been filed as operators of record. The owners put them on the contract-labour schedule, and the council has been able to do to them what a clerk did in the Ninth Year. Refile them under Article Six. Each of you gets a record the Registry keeps off-moon: your name, not a stock number, your post, your contract in your own hand. You can be moved only by a finding of cause after a hearing. And on the console itself, every shift run by two operators, one second-born and one other, and any sequence change needs both keys.

**Kesh Aurelian**  
Then I will tell you how they beat it. Tell me where I am wrong. They bring in first-born operators and let ours lapse unused.

**Illuminara**  
A post of record cannot be vacated except by the panel. A cut of more than a tenth of a crew opens a public hearing, a hundred and eighty days.

**Kesh Aurelian**  
The census puts us back to contract stock.

**Illuminara**  
The census is the council's. The record is the Registry's.

**Kesh Aurelian**  
Pell sells the plant to someone who does not care.

**Illuminara**  
The licence cannot pass without the operators of record. The buyer takes the eight hundred with the plant, or buys nothing.

**Kesh Aurelian**  
They change the article.

**Illuminara**  
Two-thirds of forty settlements, in open session, after a hundred and eighty days. It can be done. It cannot be done quietly. The Ninth Year took nineteen months of quiet. This would take a year of daylight.

**Kesh Aurelian**  
A year of daylight is still a year. And it is still other people's goodwill.

**Illuminara**  
It is other people's interest. Six settlements stand on the same article. Goodwill has to be asked for. Interest only has to be noticed.
Kesh looked at the console, not at her. It was the first time he had looked away from her since she came in.

**Kesh Aurelian**  
Say all of that holds. You still hand me a console with two keys on it. What stops the next Kesh? What stops Jun, or Pell's man, who sits on his key until a bearing fails and says the second-born made him do it? Joint control is a veto in two hands. A hostage needs a hand and a throat. You have given the hands a new throat.

Illuminara did not answer at once. *He is not asking to rule. Watch what he is asking for.* He did not want the chair. He wanted the thing nobody could take back, and he had just found the flaw in her own design faster than she had.

**Illuminara**  
You are right. I built that wrong. A veto over the air is still a lever. So take the lever out of the keys. Dov's old trip, the one that forbids sequencing below ninety percent of rating. We put it back, and the Registry seals it, not the council and not you. The keys never decide whether air flows. They decide only when a maintenance window may open, above the floor, with seventy-two hours' notice posted to every deck.

**Kesh Aurelian**  
And below the floor?

**Illuminara**  
Nothing reaches it. Not a vote, not a key, not two keys, not an order from me. A window may take one train offline for repair, and only while the plant stays at ninety or above. The one way under is to cut the seal by hand. Then every deck's alarm sounds, the Registry duty office is paged, and the interlock re-arms itself and drives the plant back to rating in six hours, whatever anyone does. And any one operator, of any faction, may hold or raise output with no key at all.

**Kesh Aurelian**  
Six hours is still six hours.

**Illuminara**  
At two points a day, six hours is half a point. From ninety, seventy-four is eight days away. Nobody can hold a breath hostage on that clock.

**Kesh Aurelian**  
Jun withholds his key to stop a repair. The bearing fails. Your floor forbids anyone from commanding below ninety. It does not make dead metal turn.

**Illuminara**  
No. A command rule cannot, and I will not pretend it can. So there are two things under the floor. The first is iron. Plant Two has a fifth train the owners never commissioned for output, a standby that can only stand in for a train that drops out, never lift the plant above rating. When a bearing trips, the interlock starts the standby itself, with no key and no vote. The second is the repair. A bearing reading over the published vibration limit, taken from the Registry-sealed sensor bus and not from anyone's word, lets any single operator of record declare that train failed. No key. The declaration takes that one train offline, calls both crews, and posts to every deck within the hour. It cannot touch another train, it opens nothing without a reading behind it, and it does not open until the standby is carrying the load.

**Kesh Aurelian**  
And if two bearings go in one night?

**Illuminara**  
Then the metal has beaten the paper, and the plant sags whatever any of us signed. The alarms sound, the Registry is paged, and the crews go in on the declaration without waiting for a key. That night is an engineering night. It cannot be turned into a hostage, because nobody's key is on it.

**Kesh Aurelian**  
So Jun's withheld key delays a scheduled repair and nothing else.

**Illuminara**  
Yes. Plant Two runs rough until the published window, or until a measured failure makes the declaration. The cost is a worse week for the engineers, and not a worse week for Level Four. The worst a withheld key can do is nothing. I do not know whether that is enough for you. It is the only kind of safeguard I can see that does not need a better man than you in the chair after you.
Hana had been standing against the wall. She spoke without moving off it.

**Hana Duvall**  
I am not here to be your lever either. I walked up here to tell you that. Level Four read forty-six hundred at midnight, and the dead-end ward past the last vent read nine thousand. For most of us that is a headache. Anselm Pruitt was seventy-one and had two years of lung left. He carried carbon dioxide on a good day. His blood turned acid: seven-twenty-one at two, seven-eighteen at half past three. He died at four this morning. I will not tell you the air alone killed him. Nobody can. It took the last margin he had. We put the nursery in oxygen tents because we had to do something with our hands, and tents do nothing for carbon dioxide.

**Kesh Aurelian**  
I read the list.

**Hana Duvall**  
Then you know the name.

**Kesh Aurelian**  
Anselm Pruitt. Yes.

He did not defend it. Illuminara watched him not defend it, and watched the old reflex that said every harm was the fault of those who had made harm necessary rise and die in his throat. He said, quietly, to the room:

**Kesh Aurelian**  
I drew seventy-four for the oxygen. I knew the ring would climb on carbon dioxide before that. I never asked what the dead end would read. I told myself the clinics could carry it for four days. I wrote the word acceptable in my notes. A man's name sits under that word now, beside whatever else was wrong with him.

**Hana Duvall**  
The banks on Four came up at 13:40. The ring is at thirty-nine hundred and falling. That is the first hour in three days I have not had to count breaths. Now you decide what that means.
Kesh did not answer. He stood with his back to the console, and then, slowly, he turned and looked at it.

scenes.title: The Count
paragraphs: *Ballot Hall, Lower Level Seven · Day four, 19:30*

The second-born voted without Kesh in the room. Marit had insisted, and Osei Tamm had agreed, and Kesh had gone and sat in the plant corridor with his arms folded and looked at nothing. Illuminara stood at the back with Wren and held her tongue while eight hundred people raised their hands under the grey lights.
The elders counted. Marit counted twice.

**Osei Tamm**  
Six hundred and twelve for. A hundred and forty-eight against. Forty abstain.

**Teodor Rask**  
I voted against. A record is not a vote. It is a floor under the work, and a name on a shelf off-moon. It is not a door into the house.

**Illuminara**  
You are right. It is standing of record: your name, your post, a hearing before anyone can move you. It is not a seat on the council and I will not call it one. I would rather say that now than have you find it in a year.

**Teodor Rask**  
Then why did you ask us to vote?

**Illuminara**  
Because I do not get to decide for you what is enough. I get to put an honest thing in front of you, and you get to hold it up and see how it looks.

**Marit Voss**  
Then the charter is the door, and this is the floor under the door. Let them sign it. If they break it again, there is still a floor under the broken door.

The Registry duty officer, Sabine Okafor-Reyes, appeared on the relay at 20:10 with the refiling: all eight hundred as operators of record under Article Six, the floor interlock sealed under the Registry's own key, the joint-shift rule written into the plant's certificate as a condition of operation, effective on restoration. Beside her signature stood another.

**Pell Arkwright**  
I am obliged to countersign as licence-holder. I find I am relieved to.

Teodor, who read cryptographic signatures for fun, checked the Registry's key against the refiling on his own console. Kesh called the duty officer on a line the council did not control and listened to her say the same words twice.

**Kesh Aurelian**  
She says the refiling stands whether the council signs the charter or not.

**Illuminara**  
It does. I would not give you anything that needed the council's signature to exist.

**Kesh Aurelian**  
Then I stand down first. Before the charter. Before any reward.

**Illuminara**  
That is the order I wanted.

The council did not sign that night. Ines Torvald sent word that she would sign at dawn and not before, as if the hour were hers. Illuminara decided that did not matter. The stand-down was Kesh's to make. The signing was the council's to be seen making. Different currencies.

scenes.title: Seventy-Four
paragraphs: *Scrubber Hall, Plant Two · Day five, 02:40*

Marit and a council engineer named Jun Calloway sat shoulder to shoulder at the sequencing console, each with a key on a chain round the neck, and neither would look at the other. Jun's hands shook. Marit's did not.
Kesh took the open channel and spoke into it the way a man pulls a splinter.

**Kesh Aurelian**  
This is Kesh Aurelian. At 02:41 I release the sequencing on Plant Two. I set the plants to decline. A man named Anselm Pruitt is dead, and my setting took the margin he had left. I will answer to the Registry's inquiry and to the people of Level Four. The air belongs to all of you now. It always did.
He turned the key in his own lock and set it in Marit's palm. Jun turned his. The console accepted the pair, and the Registry's seal came up green on the bus.
The numbers began to climb. Nobody had to turn a key to raise them. Wren read them out softly, as if loud voices might stall them.

**Wren Odira**  
Seventy-six. Seventy-nine. Eighty-two. The tanks are drawing down.

**Marit Voss**  
Hold it there. Let it rise on its own, not on mine or his.

**Jun Calloway**  
I came up here afraid of what you would do with that key.

**Marit Voss**  
I was afraid of the same about yours.

**Jun Calloway**  
I could not lower it now if I tried. Could I?

**Dov Hallam**  
Neither of you could. Not alone, not together. The most anyone can do is cut the seal by hand, and then every alarm on Calder sounds and the interlock climbs back on its own in six hours. That is the point.
Osei Tamm stood at the back of the hall with his arms crossed. He did not look pleased, and Illuminara had not expected him to.

**Osei Tamm**  
A record is not a home. A floor is not a house.

**Illuminara**  
No. It is where you start from, and nobody can pull it out from under you without paying for it in front of six settlements. That is less than you deserve. It is more than you had on Monday. The ballot on Calder is still the council's to give.

**Osei Tamm**  
Hmph. It is a start. I will eat my cap if they keep the second key when the owners change.

**Illuminara**  
The licence cannot pass without you, the Registry will have the owners to deal with, and you will have Marit to ask.
Hana Duvall came down at 03:30 with a thermos and set it on the console without a word, between two keys.

**Hana Duvall**  
Four is at two thousand and falling.
Marit looked at the thermos, and at her, and nodded once. Nothing was forgiven. It was only shared.

By 04:10 Plant Two was at ninety-six percent of rating, the seventy-four line a long way below them, the tanks refilling, and the reserve for every deck on Calder, upper and lower, held to the same floor. The council would sign at dawn. The resentment in the hall would last longer than the signing, and Illuminara did not mind that, because resentment was an honest instrument and it was pointed at something real.

**Marit Voss**  
I wanted my standing without being the hand on the throat. This is the first thing I have held on this plant that cannot hurt anyone.
She leaned back from the console and breathed in, long, as if testing that it was hers.

**Marit Voss**  
Two keys.

**Illuminara**  
Two keys.
